verses.note: The phrase ‘knowledge of good and evil’ is explained in several ways: moral autonomy (deciding good and evil for oneself), a merism for all knowledge, or the mature judgment that children lack (Deuteronomy 1:39) and the very old lose (2 Samuel 19:35). The text leaves the tree's meaning partly veiled, but the story makes clear that such knowledge was not to be seized apart from God's word.
The servant has prayed for a sign, but he does not rush to claim it. Wisdom waits and watches before concluding that God has spoken, even when the evidence seems to be arriving.

Joseph does not treat revelation as a reason for passivity. Knowing what God will do calls for planning, administration, and the right person to carry it out. Biblical wisdom is practical skill in living under God's rule.

The king's wisdom is calculation in the service of fear. Scripture sets it against the wisdom that begins with the fear of God, which the midwives will show in verse 17, and Paul later says God makes foolish the wisdom of the world (1 Corinthians 1:19-20).
Wisdom for rulers begins with recognizing whose rule theirs is under. The psalm, which opened the Psalter after the wisdom poem of Psalm 1, ends in wisdom's language.
Wisdom begins with God's counsel and becomes internal, so that the believer's own reflection carries it. Night, a time of fear elsewhere in the Psalms (Psalm 6:6), becomes a time of instruction.
Wisdom here is a gift, not an achievement, and it is inseparable from the fear of the LORD, the beginning of wisdom in Proverbs 1:7. The king's competence rests on his reverence.
The verse is wisdom teaching in the tradition of Proverbs 27:1, which warns against boasting about tomorrow. Faith does not deny trouble; it declines to borrow tomorrow's.
The saying requires the discernment that verses 1 to 5 might seem to rule out. Jesus himself told the disciples to shake the dust off their feet where they were not received (10:14).
Wisdom in the Bible is not cleverness but doing what is right and true. Jesus defines the wise person as the one who acts on his words, which makes his teaching the new measure of wisdom.
The Sermon on the Mount ends where Proverbs begins: with two ways of life and their outcomes. Hearing without doing is the fool's path.
The first mark of a faithful disciple in a time of crisis is discernment. Jesus warns against believing anyone who claims his authority simply because the claim is dramatic.
Jesus' warnings are practical. Faith does not mean staying put and waiting for rescue; it can mean fleeing when the time comes, without clinging to possessions.
The wisdom Paul prays for is directed at knowing God. Biblical wisdom begins and ends in relationship to him (Proverbs 1:7), not in cleverness about the world.

Wisdom here is knowledge of God's will aimed at a way of life (verse 10). Against teachers who promised higher knowledge, Paul prays for a knowledge that issues in faithful conduct, not in esoteric experience.
